title: Apologizing plainly
tomorrow: tara posts something mean about simran. can she forgive that?

lines: EVERY BUT SLIDES THE WEIGHT AWAY.
cards: Sorry, but. Two words that undo the first one. Simran knows exactly which buts she wants.
Sorry, but everyone was posting. Sorry, but I never sent the joke. Sorry, but it was only an emoji.
All true. All of them sliding the weight off her and back onto the chat. Her face goes hot just drafting it.
Bebe Jaswant, at the stove, doesn't turn around. Ask the way we ask at the end of Ardas, she says. No buts in it.

teach.b: Here's what Bebe means. Ardas is the prayer Sikhs say standing, hands pressed together, and tradition makes room in it to ask pardon after a reading for any mistakes: a letter added, a letter missed, a word said wrong.
Bhul chuk, slips and errors. It's said simply. Nobody explains why they slipped.

teach.h: GURU NANAK: I AM NOT GOOD.
teach.b: In the Granth, in Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak puts it even plainer: I am not good, and no one is bad. That's the posture of an apology without excuses. Not I'm the worst person alive.
Just: I'm not the good one in this story, and you're not the bad one. Feel what each version does in the body.
The excuse lifts your shoulders, ready to defend. The plain sorry lets them drop. The heat in your face is real, and it passes.
And here's the surprising part to tell a friend: the plain apology is shorter. Sorry, but takes a paragraph.
Sorry takes one breath. So Simran calls. I put a laughing face on that thread before I thought.
I'm sorry. That's all. Kiran is quiet a second.
Then: thanks for saying it like that.

how: Sikhs say Ardas standing with palms joined, and it is customary after a reading to ask pardon for any slips (bhul chuk) in it, simply and without explanation.

o: saying sorry so they'll apologize too
saying sorry without excuses or a 'but'
saying sorry in writing so it's on record

games.q: a plain sorry — tap the pairs.
p: the prayer said standing, palms joined
I am not good, and no one is bad

s: a real apology explains why you did it
every but slides the weight back off you; the pardon asked in Ardas is said simply.
in Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak says: I am not good, and no one is bad
the posture of an apology without excuses.
a plain apology means calling yourself the worst
not the worst: just not the good one in this story.

games.q: you snapped at your little brother, and you were also really tired. he's sulking in his room. what does a plain apology sound like?
o: "i'm sorry i snapped at you." then stop.
"i'm sorry, but i was exhausted and you were loud."
"i'm the worst sibling ever. i'm so, so sorry."
games.why: the tiredness is true, and it's still a but. a plain sorry owns your part in one breath, without excuses or a show of self-blame.

practice: Sit or stand tall and press your palms together at your chest, the way people stand for Ardas. Bring to mind one person you owe a plain sorry, and say it out loud, quietly, one sentence with no but.
Then let your hands rest and your shoulders drop for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Apologizing plainly. Sorry, with no but after it. Bhul chuk: slips and errors, owned.

orig.note: Punjabi: bhul chuk, slips and errors; pardon is asked for them after a reading.

carryVoice: Sorry, plainly: one breath, no but, and then let the quiet do the rest. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 728 (Suhi, Mahala 1: ham nahi changay bura nahi koe), paraphrased
